data.title: Abu Dhabi Court Orders 18 Crypto Firms Including Circle and World Liberty Financial to Keep Stolen Binance Tokens Frozen
data.description:
Abu Dhabi Judges Move to Lock Down Billions in Stolen Binance Crypto

Stolen digital tokens worth billions of dollars now sit under a court-ordered freeze in Abu Dhabi, as Binance pushes to claw back what thieves took from its wallets.

The Abu Dhabi Global Market (ADGM) Courts have told 18 crypto firms, including Circle and World Liberty Financial, to keep their hold on tokens linked to the theft.

The raid on 29 October 2026 drained about $6.3 billion from Binance wallets, making it the largest crypto heist on record.

🚨BINANCE SAYS IT HAS COURT ORDER FROM ABU DHABI TO RECOVER FROZEN TOKENS FROM RECENT HACK!@binance says it secured a court order from the Abu Dhabi Global Market as part of its efforts to recover tokens that were frozen after the big hack, according to Reuters.

The exchange… pic.twitter.com/crfynagH2N

— Crypto Banter (@crypto_banter) November 18, 2026

Who Has Been Told to Keep the Tokens Frozen?

Circle, which issues the dollar-linked stablecoin USDC, and World Liberty Financial, the crypto venture run by the family of US President Donald Trump, head the list of named companies.

The court was careful to say that none of the 18 firms is accused of wrongdoing.

Many had already frozen the tokens before the order arrived.

Under the ruling, they must maintain those freezes until further proceedings.

They are also barred from lending or swapping the tokens, or mixing them with other assets.

The order is an interim measure to protect assets Binance says belong to it, and it does not decide who finally gets the money back.

A further hearing on 1 December 2026 will weigh whether the injunction should continue and on what terms.

Binance recovery: An Abu Dhabi court ordered 18 cryptocurrency companies to preserve frozen assets connected to October's $6.3 billion Binance wallet theft. Binance says approximately $2.85 billion has been frozen or intercepted.

— Fizy Xchange💙🦅 (@FizyXchange) November 19, 2026

Why Is Tether Missing From the Order?

Tether, the El Salvador-based issuer of the USDT token, is not among the named companies, even though it earlier said it had frozen $1.5 billion of the stolen funds.

Binance says it is working with Tether directly on returning those assets.

A Tether spokesperson said:

"In consultation with the relevant authorities, we will work directly with Binance in respect of reissuing the tokens."

Binance said on 3 November that around $2.85 billion of the stolen tokens had been frozen or intercepted by third parties.

Stablecoins from Tether and Circle can be frozen by their issuers, but bitcoin is far harder to pull back once it moves, unless it lands at an exchange or service willing to cooperate.

How Big Is the Wider Court Package?

A separate account of the proceedings describes a much larger set of orders.

According to it, Justice William Stone SBS KC granted a worldwide freezing injunction with a stated value of $6.5 billion against unidentified people alleged to have carried out the fraud.

That figure is the amount covered by the order, not money already recovered.

Binance has not said how much of the stolen crypto has come back through the court action.

The package also includes interim proprietary injunctions and delivery-up orders against different groups of unidentified defendants, plus interim orders against named defendants that had frozen some of the assets.

Gibson Dunn, the US law firm acting for Binance, called the injunction "one of, if not the, largest publicly known freezing orders ever made."

Can a Court Order Chase Stolen Crypto Across Blockchains?

The orders try to answer that with technology.

They allow court papers to be served through the blockchain itself, and they rely on a constantly updated "living list" of about 26,000 wallet addresses said to hold stolen assets.

🚨 BINANCE JUST WON A 6.5BILLIONFREEZEORDER!

⚖️AbuDhabi'sADGMCourtsissuedaworldwidefreezinginjunctionagainsttheunknownOct29hackers
🔗Itcoversa"livinglist"of~26,000walletsandcanbeservedON-CHAIN
🧊~2.85B of the ~$6.34B stolen was already frozen… pic.twitter.com/OQuj0wYfcC

— BodLaim (@Bodlaim_) November 19, 2026

M. Kendall Day of Gibson Dunn explained:

"Just as significant is how the orders will work in practice: they can be served via the blockchain, and the market will be notified of a constantly updating 'living list' of 26,000 wallet addresses identified as holding stolen assets, enabling those assets to be frozen rapidly even as they are laundered at pace."

The paperwork also matters for a practical reason.

Some issuers and exchanges need formal judicial approval before they release or return frozen funds, and the ADGM orders give them that cover.

🔰 BINANCE STRIKES BACK! A $6.5 BILLION GLOBAL FREEZING ORDER!

There's a major breakthrough in the aftermath of the October 29 hack.@binance has secured a worldwide asset-freezing injunction from Abu Dhabi Global Market (ADGM) Courts, covering up to $6.5 BILLION in assets… https://t.co/YncIgBiLBxpic.twitter.com/8vAby8VRVM

— FrontierX 🔶 (@RealFrontierX) November 19, 2026

What Does Binance Say About Its Customers?

Binance says users have not lost out.

The company covered the stolen assets from its own reserves, including its emergency fund SAFU and its corporate treasury, and has resumed withdrawals in phases.

Dugan Bliss, the firm's deputy general counsel, said:

"We will continue using every lawful tool available to trace, freeze and recover stolen assets, support our partners in returning funds where possible, and keep those assets out of the hands of the attackers."

Abu Dhabi is Binance's global hub, and the company counts the ADGM's Financial Services Regulatory Authority as its main regulator.

SB Seker, its Asia-Pacific head, told the Singapore Fintech Festival that the company plans to enter five Asian markets in 2027 and needs no new fundraising after the hack.

"The cost of covering the stolen tokens is not a large amount for us statistically. The impact is manageable, and we can get through it without changing how we operate."

Talks with three of those markets are nearing the final stage, with details due in the first quarter of 2027.

How Did the Attackers Get In?

Binance says the attack took months to prepare.

In June, tampered software in an installer compromised an engineer's device.

In September, another engineer was approached by someone posing as a recruiter and was tricked into running a fake interview task that carried malware.

The attackers then reached the company's internal wallet-signing service and, on 29 October, emptied hot wallets across several blockchains.

The haul included about 233.46 million XRP, about 975,000 SOL and about 18,270 BTC.

Binance says it has covered every asset hit by the 29 October hack. It paid for that out of its own funds.

Getting the stolen coins back is a separate track. Binance's blog of 3 November puts the impact at about 6.34billion,including18,270BTC and 233.46 million $XRP sent… pic.twitter.com/rIl630RxA0

— Yieldr.io (@yieldr_official) November 14, 2026

Blockchain analysis suggests the thieves tried to swap stablecoins into ether quickly but could not outrun the issuers' freezes.

The FBI and Binance have both pointed to North Korea's "TraderTraitor" group, while Pyongyang has denied any role.

Could This Case Become a Template for the Industry?

Stablecoin issuers have frozen assets at the request of authorities before, but a court ordering many firms to hold a freeze at once is unusual.

Market watchers see the Abu Dhabi order as a possible model for protecting assets after future thefts.

It also shows how hard it remains to recover decentralised assets such as bitcoin.

For Binance, much now rests on the 1 December hearing and on how many of the frozen tokens can be returned.

data.title: Anthropic's IPO is finally complete: valuation reaches $1.5 trillion.
data.description:
Anthropic's IPO price was set at $83, valuing the company at approximately $1.5 trillion. Excluding the transfer of existing shares, the company expects to raise approximately $79 billion, surpassing SpaceX to become the largest IPO in history. The stock will begin trading on Thursday under the ticker symbol "ANT".

On Wednesday evening local time, Anthropic announced that the IPO would sell 155 million more shares than initially expected, expanding its already record-breaking IPO size by nearly $13 billion.

The AI ​​lab will issue a total of 980 million shares, compared to 825 million shares in its latest prospectus.

Anthropic's IPO price was set at $83, higher than the previously indicated range of $70-$78. Trading began on Thursday under the ticker symbol "ANT". On a fully diluted basis, the offering is expected to value the company at approximately $1.5 trillion. In line with market expectations, only a small portion of the shares (approximately 23.6 million shares) came from existing shareholders. Excluding the transfer of existing shares, the company expects to raise approximately $79 billion, surpassing SpaceX to become the largest IPO in history. In June, SpaceX issued 555.6 million shares at $135, raising $75 billion. In addition to this $79 billion, Anthropic is expected to complete a $26 billion private placement (subscribed by Nvidia, Google, Microsoft, Micron, AMD, TSMC, and Broadcom), bringing its total post-IPO fundraising to $105 billion. Furthermore, the underwriting banks have an over-allotment option to purchase additional shares. This major IPO is even bigger than before. Anthropic: The First Pure AI Lab to Go Public on the US Stock Market. While many other publicly traded companies, including Meta, Alphabet, and SpaceX, are developing large-scale AI models, Anthropic will become the first company whose entire business revolves around AI research and development. The company continuously iterates and upgrades the Claude model, providing services through its own platform and third-party cloud vendors, and developing various application products based on the model. This cycle continues. Dan Ives, a technology analyst who is bullish on AI, wrote in a research report on Wednesday: "This is the first time a leading US AI lab has had an independent public market valuation." He added that this valuation "has not been muddied by its advertising or rocket business." Anthropic is unlikely to remain alone for long; its main competitor, OpenAI, has also filed confidential IPO documents with the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC), but is not expected to go public until 2027. Anthropic shares have been "frozen" for some time. The biggest winners of Anthropic's rapid growth are the early investors who entered the market before its IPO. Since completing its Series G funding round in February at a valuation of $380 billion, Anthropic's market capitalization has almost quadrupled. However, investors wanting to buy and sell shares before the IPO have not had an easy time. Several private equity firms have stated that their private trading activity has been very quiet in recent months. Anthropic explicitly stated in May that it would not approve any share transfers without the company's approval. Greg Martin, managing director of private brokerage firm Rainmaker Securities, said this warning was like "pouring cold water" on over-the-counter trading. “If you’re a buyer, you don’t want to buy something that isn’t recognized,” Martin told Barron’s; and if you’re a seller holding shares in this high-value company, “the last thing you want is to create complications.” Early investors’ shares will still be subject to a lock-up period of several months after the IPO, which is a standard IPO arrangement, but they are now one step closer to realizing their gains. The $1.5 trillion valuation is an equilibrium result of multiple parties’ negotiations. The $1.5 trillion valuation falls within a comfortable range between the upper and lower limits of investor expectations. This summer, there were rumors that its valuation could reach $2 trillion, but subsequently, the AI ​​sector weakened, and investors lowered their expectations. Anthropic itself remained silent on this matter until last week when it announced its offering price range of $70 to $78. The final IPO price of $83 indicates strong market demand for Anthropic stock, but the valuation wasn't so high as to deter potential investors. "I think this shows that people have a huge appetite for exposure to the long-term trend of 'smart' technology," said David Fetherstonhaugh, chief investment officer at asset management firm VistaShares, regarding the final pricing. Is Anthropic's stock price expensive? Currently, Wall Street's assessment of Anthropic is still limited. Investment banks involved in the IPO typically wait two to three weeks to release their research reports. Of course, brokerages not involved in the IPO can comment on the valuation. Pierre Ferragu, an analyst at New Street Research, has already initiated coverage. He predicts that Anthropic's EBITDA will reach $183 billion by 2030. Based on its IPO pricing, Anthropic's valuation is approximately 8 times its projected 2030 EBITDA. Whether this price is worthwhile is difficult to determine. In comparison, SpaceX's valuation is approximately 4 times its estimated 2030 EBITDA. The S&P 500's valuation is approximately 13 times its projected 12-month EBITDA. Currently, there is no reliable estimate of the S&P 500's 2030 EBITDA. The extremely high growth expectations provide some support for AI valuations, but 2030 is still a long way off, and the industry is changing rapidly. A key figure Anthropic investors should pay attention to: After its IPO, Anthropic will be required to disclose quarterly financial reports. Going forward, investors should closely monitor its "computing cost gross margin"—that is, the gross profit after deducting computing power costs. According to the prospectus, Anthropic's third-quarter revenue was approximately $17 billion, a year-on-year surge of 1127%; computing power investment was close to $10 billion, with a remaining profit of approximately $7.1 billion after deducting computing power costs, resulting in a computing power gross margin of 42%. In the second quarter, this gross margin was 52%. This stronger gross margin indicates strong pricing and demand for Anthropic's services; it also means that Anthropic needs more computing power—which is crucial for AI computing power service providers like SpaceX and CoreWeave. It's difficult to predict where the gross margin will ultimately stabilize. Finding companies with quarterly revenues of tens of billions of dollars and growth rates exceeding 1000% for comparison is not easy. Anthropic's IPO May Displace Nvidia's Leading Position in AI, Diverting Tech Funds

Market attention is entirely focused on Anthropic. Some investors believe that the upcoming IPO of Anthropic could replace Nvidia as the new leader in AI deals.

Typically, new stocks are not discussed in terms of whether they pose a significant challenge to established companies, especially when the competitor is a company with a peak market capitalization of nearly $5 trillion.

However, the resignation of Nvidia's founder and former CEO Jensen Huang due to scandal has prompted investors to speculate that Anthropic could become the new king of AI. If this prediction comes true, funds will be sold off from other tech stocks and used to increase holdings in Anthropic.

Some investors say that Nvidia's institutional shareholders (whether they have already reduced their holdings or still hold Nvidia positions) are eager to buy Anthropic shares.

An advisor who placed orders with clients for this IPO stated that the funds entering ANT must have a source, and the funds withdrawn from Nvidia seem to be a logical one. Amazon and Google hold large stakes, but their voting rights are not significant. Combined, Amazon and Google will likely hold more than 35% of Anthropic's shares in the future. After the IPO and concurrent private placement, Google will hold 1.8 billion shares. At $74 per share, this corresponds to an equity value of approximately $133 billion. Amazon initially holds 1.9 billion shares and also holds convertible bonds in Anthropic. If all of these are exercised and converted into shares, Amazon will hold a maximum of 3.5 billion shares, equivalent to a value of approximately $260 billion at $74 per share. Together, they represent 28.4% of the issued common stock; if Amazon converts all of its bonds, its combined shareholding is estimated to reach 36%. However, the significant shareholdings of the two companies do not grant them much formal governance power within Anthropic. Anthropic employs a complex shareholding structure, with the seven founders retaining a combined 50.1% of the voting rights. In most major votes, Class A shareholders, including existing shareholders and IPO new share buyers, hold only 49.9% of the voting rights. Amazon and Google hold Class N shares, specifically reserved for business partners. These shares do not have regular voting rights unless converted into Class A shares through sale or transfer. Nevertheless, these two companies remain deeply tied to Anthropic's success or failure, enjoying substantial economic benefits. Besides Google and Amazon, Nvidia, AMD, Broadcom, Micron, Microsoft, and TSMC also participated in the subscription. Analysts: Anthropic is a "once-in-a-generation IPO" This AI company, backed by Claude's grand model, has already garnered bullish ratings from Wall Street institutions even before its IPO pricing has been finalized. New Street Research analyst Pierre Ferragu was the first to initiate coverage of Anthropic, giving it a "buy" rating and a target price of $105. This bullish report was released on the eve of Anthropic's listing. "Anthropic is a 'once-in-a-generation' IPO. We expect AI's share of knowledge work-related spending to continue to rise over the next few decades, just as cloud computing's share of IT spending has steadily increased since 2010," Ferragu said. In his view, the only difference is that AI "is adopting at twice the speed of cloud computing, and its potential market size is ten times larger." Ferragu estimates the current potential market size for AI to be $35 trillion, expanding to $50 trillion by 2030. He believes that Anthropic, with its self-developed AI models, is in a leading position in the industry and is expected to deliver solid operating results after its IPO. The analyst predicts that Anthropic's cash burn will remain low; revenue will reach $500 billion by 2030, with an EBIT margin of approximately 15%.

data.title: Musk connects Shenzhen with New York: Getting rid of Huang Renxun is like kicking out Jordan.
data.description:
On the morning of November 19th, Elon Musk, who had just arrived in Shenzhen, held a video conference with the Dealbook Summit in New York from his hotel room. The conversation began around 6:50 AM and lasted approximately 45 minutes. The interviewer was Andrew Ross Sorkin, founder of the Dealbook Summit. Topics included Musk's trip to China; Nvidia's dismissal of Jensen Huang; the US midterm elections and Musk's reflections; and the merger of SpaceX and Tesla. This article is based on the complete interview video, with some fragmented sentences and interjections removed, and some necessary deletions made. The full text is approximately 7,000 words.

The following, enjoy:

I'm a huge China fan

Sorkin: There's a lot to talk about today, and you're in China with the president right now.

Musk: Yes, I just got here. I mean, every time I come to China, I'm blown away. Honestly, it's an impressive country. I'm in Shenzhen right now, it's a huge city with really cool architecture, and I think it's the biggest hub for advanced technology in China. Every time I come here, I'm overwhelmed by the scale and grandeur of China. I'm a China fan. I always encourage people to come to China and see for themselves.

This is a very impressive country, and I'm a huge fan. One of the reasons I came here is to visit the Tesla Shanghai factory and thank the team for their incredible hard work over the years and the excellent vehicles they produce. Also, the president is here, and they are discussing trade relations; I hope they achieve some results. I believe that good trade and relations between the US and China would be a good thing for the world. Getting rid of Jensen Huang is like kicking Michael Jordan out of the Bulls. Sorkin: I want to talk about something we've discussed with almost every guest today. You've been at the forefront of this issue because he's a good friend of yours, and you've publicly discussed the idea of ​​bringing Jensen Huang back to Nvidia; if you can't bring him back, have you considered bringing him back yourself? What do you think? Musk: Yes, I think I've always been very frank online, and I think everyone can see that. Jensen Huang is an old friend of mine. I would compare him to someone like Michael Jordan, probably at his peak, in terms of what he means to a team. You really have to think carefully before letting someone like that go. For example, if you're the Chicago Bulls, in the middle of your second season, on a winning streak, and you kick Michael Jordan out of the team—in my opinion, that's not a wise decision. No one can truly replace Jensen Huang. He does the work of several people. He manages the supply chain. You'll see him eating street food with key suppliers. He's built long-term relationships with these people over decades. He has an extremely deep understanding of technology. His team loves him, loves him very much. Many people stayed because of him; they turned down higher offers elsewhere because of their personal loyalty to Jensen Huang. Before kicking someone like that out, you really need to think twice. I know he made some mistakes in this matter. But I don't think he's disloyal to America. I've said it publicly: it's like you're on a winning streak and you kick Michael Jordan out of the team—it's not a good thing for shareholders. You have to weigh the benefits a person brings against the harm they cause. So, yes, I think it was a mistake. I've said it publicly, and many people have said it too. Sorkin: You said it yourself, you would hire him. The board… Musk: Of course, but who wouldn't? He's one of the most talented entrepreneurial CEOs in history. Who wouldn't want to hire Jensen Huang? Of course, Jensen Huang is clearly not looking for a job. I think he's still a bit shocked by these things. It felt like a movie, like a George R.R. Martin script, where a main character you've become emotionally invested in suddenly disappears—it's quite shocking. Sorkin: What do you think will happen to him in the long run? Have you spoken to him about this privately? Musk: Yes. Sorkin: What did he say to you? What do you think will happen next? Musk: I don't know what will happen next. The decision is, of course, in the hands of the Nvidia board. Above that, perhaps the shareholders; but for shareholders to have any influence, it would likely require either the current board to change its mind or for shareholders to elect the board off at the shareholders' meeting—a rather rare occurrence. So, the board is still the one truly in charge. Sorkin: You're with the president now. Have you spoken to him about this? Musk: We probably shouldn't turn this interview into a "Huang Renxun interview." Sorkin: I know. Musk: Okay. I think the president has publicly stated that he believes Huang Renxun should continue as CEO. Almost everyone I know thinks so too. But ultimately, it was a decision made by Nvidia's board of directors. We're not on the board. I feel pretty stupid for losing the midterm elections. Sorkin: Right. Let me ask you something. I'll be talking about your companies later, SpaceX, Tesla, etc. You strongly supported the Republicans in the midterm elections, and they lost. I'd like to hear your reaction to this defeat: what impact do you think it will have on the country, and what impact will it have on your businesses? Now Texas has a Democratic governor, the first time in a long time. What do you think? Musk: First of all, I think the new governor will actually be quite moderate. I don't think she'll be a far-left governor. Based on everything I've heard so far, I think Texas will be fine under Gina Hinojosa. I think it will be fine in that respect. I do think it's a good thing to have some checks and balances. I didn't elaborate on my goals on X. So what was my real goal? By the way, that goal obviously failed: to get the Republicans 51 seats in the Senate. But obviously, the Republicans were crushed in this election. The money I spent—I think I was pretty stupid, spending so much money and not seeing much effect; of course, maybe it would have been worse without that money. But it really shows that elections in America aren't just about money. You can obviously throw a lot of money into an election and have relatively limited results, and I think that was the case this time. So if I could turn back the clock, I would probably have spent less money. I personally wouldn't have put a lot of energy into this, because my focus is on building SpaceX, Tesla, and those things.

I don't think I need a pardon

Sorkin: I'm asking this to see if you think this will impact your company. Because you hear people like the chairman of the oversight committee saying "go to a lawyer"; you hear the president saying, "If I had to give him a pardon"—referring to you—"I would give him a pardon." I'm asking from a personal perspective.

Musk: By the way, I don't think I need a pardon because I haven't committed any crimes. I understand your question. But some of these people are going a bit too far. Some Democrats, I remember even the incoming Texas House Majority Leader saying I should go to jail. Then someone asked him: What crime? He couldn't name a single crime.

Musk: By the way, I don't think I need a pardon because I haven't committed any crimes.

Musk: By the way, I don't think I need a pardon because I haven't committed any crimes.

Starlink, Starship, and the Future of Multiplanetary

Sorkin: Talk about Starlink. I recently saw that you also plan to do terrestrial phone service. What does this ultimately mean for Verizon, T-Mobile, and AT&T? There are many questions: How easy is it to do? How much will it cost? What do you envision the future look like?

Musk: We want to do something useful in communications. These useful communications services will allow us to fund the development of advanced rockets like Starship. We built Starlink, and its benefit is providing high-bandwidth, low-cost connectivity to areas of the world that didn't exist before. We've already provided high-bandwidth, affordable connectivity to many rural schools and hospitals, and to relief organizations. Countless lives have been saved by Starlink—because ships were sinking at sea, or natural disasters had occurred, and Starlink was the only means of communication. I'm not sure of the exact number, but I think it's probably hundreds. Hundreds of lives were saved because, in natural disasters, or as I just mentioned, for those lost or on airplanes, Starlink was the only means of connectivity. It's all over the internet; you can find out how good Starlink has been by searching online. It's also the first global high-bandwidth system ever built. But Starlink has another important long-term role: we need some way to fund rockets capable of extending life as we know it, extending consciousness beyond Earth, to ensure the long-term survival of humanity, consciousness, and life as we understand it by building self-sustaining cities on the Moon and Mars. Because anything could happen on Earth—nuclear war, a massive meteorite, a supervolcano, or some kind of bioengineered virus. Sorkin: Do you think that kind of thing could really happen? Is that what really drives you? Is it what you fear? Musk: You just need to look at the fossil record, look at how many extinction events have happened—lots of them—and you'll know it's just a matter of time, a "when" rather than a "whether." I categorize these as "defensive reasons": extending life and consciousness beyond Earth. These are all important, like insuring life as a whole, a kind of life insurance that covers everything. But if you ask me what motivates me more than that, I would say: I want to see an exciting future—where we venture out to explore new frontiers, to new star systems, and where science fiction isn't just fiction forever. We should be brave enough to go, like in Star Trek, to places no one has ever been before. Maybe we'll discover some long-extinct alien civilizations, maybe we'll find real aliens we can talk to. Being surrounded by stars, I think, is a future worth looking forward to, an incredibly exciting future. How do you judge whether something in the future is really cool? Ask your children, they'll tell you. There are many problems and difficulties in this world that need to be solved, but life can't just be one miserable problem after another. There must be something that excites you about the future, something that makes you happy when you wake up in the morning, something that makes you eager to see what happens next. Becoming a civilization capable of navigating among the stars is one of those things. Sorkin: Let's go back to telecommunications. One reason for doing all this is to raise funds for that future? But I'd like to ask, the cost itself is enormous. I'm also wondering if you'll eventually buy a telecom company in the US. Those companies' stock prices have fallen, and their profit margins and valuation multiples are far lower than yours. So I'd like to understand the longer-term logic. Musk: I think we already have a plan to achieve widespread, ubiquitous access on Earth, including through mobile phones. We'll start launching SpaceX's second-generation direct-to-cell constellation next year, and I think its bandwidth will be about 40 times that of the current first generation, which is a very large multiple; there will be a third generation after that, and so on. It can connect directly from space to your regular phone without requiring anything to the phone. But there's still one piece of the puzzle missing: if you're indoors, especially with a metal roof, it blocks signals from space. So we need some kind of ground infrastructure to address the situation where people are in buildings with thick roofs. That's where the 800 MHz band we bought comes in. We can build what I call micro-ground stations, very small ground stations, and in one way, bundle them with Starlink terminals to create a network. Basically, instead of erecting those huge cell towers everywhere, we're spreading out a large number of micro base stations in densely populated areas. We already have the design, and I think it will be in production next year—a rather revolutionary microcellular device that can be placed directly on the roof like a Starlink antenna to solve the problem of reaching users inside buildings. By the way, I don't think this means AT&T, Verizon, or any other company will go bankrupt. They might lose some revenue, but I think the future demand for bandwidth will be enormous, and that demand will be primarily driven by superintelligence and robots. They will need far more bandwidth than humans: the peak bandwidth for human speech is only about 100 bits per second, while computers can reach a trillion bits per second. So you'll really need several orders of magnitude more bandwidth to serve future superintelligence and massive numbers of robots. Sorkin: You probably can't talk too much, but obviously the biggest news right now is the potential merger of SpaceX and Tesla. I'm curious: what if the deal falls through? I think everyone believes that eventually a way will be found; but if it doesn't work out, how difficult do you think it will be to operate these businesses separately in the future? Musk: I think both paths are viable. It's just that there's more and more overlap or intersection between SpaceX and Tesla that didn't exist before. If you had asked me five years ago if there was any point in SpaceX and Tesla coming together, I would have said no. People asked me that too, and I said I couldn't see any logic in it. The term "synergy" has been overused and misused. Moreover, mergers where the merged company is actually more valuable than the original two companies combined are relatively rare. What we're seeing now is that artificial intelligence and robotics, or rather, superintelligence (SI) and robotics, are creating this convergence. Both SpaceX and Tesla have large AI software teams. Tesla's AI software team primarily works on real-world AI, used in Tesla's Autopilot and Optimus robots; SpaceX, on the other hand, has AI for large-scale models. Beyond AI software, both Tesla and SpaceX have advanced chip design teams. Looking further ahead, orbital computing power will truly be the direction for large-scale deployment. In the future, the supercomputing power in space will round up to 100%. I know this sounds absurd, but please remember this: I believe that the supercomputing power (remaining on the ground) will eventually account for less than 0.4% of all computing power, therefore orbital computing power will round up to 100%. I think this is a fairly easy prediction to make; it's just a matter of time. Sorkin: So you think it's necessary to combine the two companies to make this happen? Musk: It's not necessary to combine them. But wouldn't they be better together? Probably. This isn't a "merge no matter what" situation. These all require shareholder votes, and success or failure is uncertain—at least for Tesla. Even in my vote at SpaceX, I have to represent other shareholders and can't drag them into a merger that's financially detrimental to them, because I would obviously be sued. So the question is: would SpaceX and Tesla be better together, creating more value than they would have been separately? Does this assumption hold up under scrutiny? That's for the shareholders to decide. But there are so many areas of convergence that didn't exist in the past but are becoming increasingly important for the future.

Mergers shouldn't bring additional rewards

Sorkin: I have a rather pointed question. We asked everyone if they had any questions for you, and one question kept coming up.

It relates to the merger of SpaceX and Tesla, and also to your performance-based compensation package at Tesla: at least under the past arrangement, you could have received that portion of your compensation if the deal had gone through. They repeatedly asked: this was designed so you could control Tesla; now you have complete control of SpaceX. If the deal goes through, do you think you should receive that portion of your compensation? Musk: I don't think I should receive any form of reward simply for doing a merger. That's neither reasonable nor justifiable. The right way to look at any agreement is to ask: what were the parties' original intentions when they reached the agreement? You should honor the agreement and keep your word. So, for example, those Tesla stock options that depend on Tesla's performance: I shouldn't receive those option awards just because of the merger with SpaceX, because that doesn't conform to the original agreement—the agreement was that I could only receive these options because of Tesla's performance, not just because of a merger.

Cybercab and Autonomous Driving

Sorkin: Okay. There's been a lot of talk about cars lately, especially about the Cybertruck. Apparently, you're phasing it out to free up more capacity for ride-sharing services, which I guess will eventually be Cybercab. Do you think you'll continue making cars in the end? By the way, I just ordered a Tesla, but I haven't actually received it yet; the waiting list is really long.

Musk: Which model did you order?

Sorkin: YL (Model Y extended version).

Musk: That's definitely our most popular car. So I think we'll probably convert all Model Y production to Model YL, because that seems to be what most people want. Sorkin: But the question is, do you think you'll still be selling cars to individuals in the future, or once that business takes off, will you only make Cybercab? Musk: No. For us, it's still necessary to make cars that can seat different numbers of people. The Cybercab is two-seater and covers about 90% of passenger mileage. If you look at all passenger mileage, the average number of people in a car is about 1.2, so the two-seater Cybercab covers about 90% of passenger mileage. But we still need autonomous vehicles to handle groups of one family or four or six people. So we plan to make an autonomous version of the Model Y without a steering wheel and pedals to transport groups of six or seven people.

Computing Power Collaboration with Anthropic

Sorkin: I know you have some meetings to attend, and it's morning there. I'll just ask a few quick questions related to AI. You recently said that you think many of these "neoclouds" will become "guppies," and some of them won't be financially viable. I'd like you to elaborate, especially since Anthropic is going public tonight. By the way, I'd also like to hear your thoughts on Anthropic. Interestingly, you once thought this company was terrible to Western civilization, but now they're renting a lot of computing power from you. Musk: Yes. By the way, before we leased any computing power to them, I met with a lot of people at Anthropic, and we didn't just push the deal forward immediately. The fact is, I've known quite a few people at Anthropic since my days at OpenAI. Of the people I've met, none of them triggered my "evil detector." And these are relatively short-term contracts that either party can terminate. If I felt Anthropic was doing something very bad for the world, I would obviously terminate those contracts. Similarly, Anthropic can also terminate contracts, depending on the specific contract, with three to six months' notice. Sorkin: Do you think they will terminate them? Because there's some speculation, supposedly they've told some investors they might. Musk: I don't think they're likely to do that. I spoke with Anthropic, and they told me they're very likely to continue leasing computing power from SpaceX, and in fact, they want significantly more. But they also have to clarify that in the worst-case scenario, if extreme limitations are imposed on what artificial intelligence or superintelligence (SI) can do, they might not be able to use that computing power. However, they told me that in their most probable scenario, they hope to add another 10 gigawatts of computing power from SpaceX. That's a huge number. So far, my interactions with the Anthropic team have been: they seem like good people and principled. They may have some quirks, like we all do, but they seem hardworking and concerned about the future. Frankly, I like these people. So overall, it looks good, and they've certainly made some excellent AI. Opus is a great product.

Are you calm right now?

Sorkin: Perhaps I'll ask you two more philosophical questions. When we last met—I was just curious about your current personal state. Last time we were here, I talked to you about how you said your mind was like a storm. I asked you then if that was an unhappy storm. I'm curious to know what it's like now.

Musk: I think it's not always a storm. Maybe sometimes it's stormy weather, sometimes it's not. I'm not particularly stormy right now. I feel relatively calm.

Sorkin: You feel relatively calm?

Musk: Yes. Sorkin: Elon Musk. Thank you. Thank you very much for the conversation. Musk: Thank you.

data.title: NVIDIA Faces Ransomware Threat, but Breach Claims Remain Unverified
data.description:
A 10-Day Countdown Raises Questions

NVIDIA has been listed on the dark-web extortion website of ransomware group The Gentlemen, which is threatening to release allegedly stolen data within approximately 10 days. The listing, posted on 18 November, includes a countdown timer and a contact channel for ransom negotiations.

However, the group has yet to publish any evidence of the alleged breach. No sample files, data inventory, or technical details identifying the affected systems or business units have been provided. The listing alone does not establish that NVIDIA's internal network has been compromised.

NVIDIA Investigates a Possible Third-Party Incident

NVIDIA said it is investigating an incident that may have affected a third-party partner. The company stated that it has found no indication its own systems or networks were affected and that it continues to monitor the situation.

The statement leaves open the possibility that the incident could involve a supplier, contractor, or external partner rather than NVIDIA's core infrastructure. The relationship between the third-party investigation and The Gentlemen's extortion claim has not yet been conclusively established.

Why Researchers Are Urging Caution

Cybersecurity researchers have cautioned against accepting ransomware claims at face value. The Gentlemen has previously been accused of exaggerating attack claims, misattributing stolen information to organisations, or reusing previously exposed data.

Without verifiable samples, investigators cannot determine the authenticity, origin, sensitivity, or volume of the alleged stolen information. Even if data eventually emerges, further investigation would be required to confirm whether it originated from NVIDIA, a partner, or another source.

The group reportedly operates a ransomware-as-a-service (RaaS) model, allowing affiliates to carry out attacks using its tools and infrastructure. Such leak-site listings are commonly used to pressure organisations into negotiations, regardless of whether the full extent of an intrusion has been established.

The Wider Risk of Third-Party Exposure

The incident highlights a persistent cybersecurity challenge: organisations can face data exposure through their wider supply chain, even when their own systems remain uncompromised.

Partners, cloud providers, contractors and software vendors may have access to business information, credentials or operational systems. A security weakness within one of these external environments can potentially create risks for multiple organisations.

Companies should therefore review third-party access privileges, monitor data-sharing arrangements, enforce strong authentication, and ensure that vendors meet cybersecurity and incident-reporting requirements.

Conclusion: A Threat Is Not Proof of a Breach

The NVIDIA case remains an evolving cybersecurity incident, with the ransomware group's allegations yet to be substantiated. The countdown may be intended to increase pressure on the company, but it is not evidence that sensitive information has been stolen.

Until verified data or further official findings emerge, organisations and the public should distinguish between ransomware claims and confirmed security incidents. The case also serves as a reminder that cybersecurity resilience extends beyond an organisation's internal network to every partner and service provider connected to its operations.

data.title: South Korea to Ban Private Lenders From Offering General Personal Loans to Soldiers After Borrowing Jumps 69 Times in Three Years
data.description:
From Barracks Bunks to Borrowed Millions: Why Korea Is Curbing Loans to Soldiers

A corporal posted a request on an online platform that links borrowers with private moneylenders last November.

He was due to leave the army the following June and already owed about 20 million won ($15,000) to banks, savings banks and other lenders.

His question was short:

"Is there anywhere I could get my hands on 5 million won?"

His plea is now a regular sight on such sites, and South Korea's financial regulator has decided to act.

The Financial Supervisory Service (FSS) intends to bar private lenders from offering general-purpose personal loans to active-duty servicemen.

🇰🇷 JUST IN: South Korea plans to restrict high-interest loans to active-duty soldiers after borrowings hit ₩24.2B (~$17M), linked to crypto and online gambling.

— CryptoMeter.io (@CryptoMeterIO) November 15, 2026

How Did Lending to Soldiers Grow So Fast?

The numbers show how quickly the market expanded.

According to the Financial Services Commission, the 30 largest registered loan companies lent 24.2 billion won ($17.5 million) to active-duty servicemen in 2025.

That compares with 350 million won ($254,000) in 2022, a rise of almost 69 times in three years.

Regulators link the jump to easier access to online betting and speculative investment.

Soldiers have been allowed to use smartphones after duty hours since 2020, which has put gambling sites within reach of the barracks.

Higher pay has added to the mix.

A sergeant's monthly compensation has more than doubled, from 676,100 won ($490) in 2022 to 1.5 million won ($1,090) this year.

군대 간 아들 있는 집은 이거 한 번 보셈
병장 월급이 두 배 되는 동안 병사 대출은 69배 뛰었음

1. 상위 30개 대부업체 현역병 대출: 2022년 말 3억5천만원 → 작년 말 242억원
2. 병장 월급은 67만6천원 → 올해 150만원
3. 은행·저축은행은 현역병 신용대출 안 해줌. 근데 일부 대부업체가… pic.twitter.com/nfA2rLCtMY

— 펌질하는고닉 (@PJG0012e) November 18, 2026

Why Can Private Lenders Reach Soldiers That Banks Cannot?

Mainstream lenders such as banks and savings banks generally refuse unsecured personal loans to serving soldiers, who cannot provide the usual income documents.

Private lenders have filled the gap by accepting copies of military pay account statements as proof of income.

That practice is the target of the new rule.

The proposal was discussed on 12 November at the fifth meeting of the Financial Consumer Protection Advisory Committee, chaired by FSS Governor Lee Chan-jin, and the regulator confirmed it on 15 November.

The FSS has agreed with the Korea Consumer Loan Finance Association to add the ban to the industry's standard operating guidelines by the end of the year.

Enforcement will rely on industry self-regulation, and the FSS will work with the Financial Services Commission and the banking sector to finalise the details.

Not every loan will be blocked.

Collateralised loans and small emergency cash loans will remain available, as the authorities accept that soldiers may need money quickly for living costs.

병장 월급이 두 배 되는 동안 병사 대출은 69배 뛰었음

1. 상위 30개 대부업체 현역병 대출: 2022년 말 3억5천만원 → 작년 말 242억원
2. 병장 월급은 67만6천원 → 올해 150만원
3. 은행·저축은행은 현역병 신용대출 안 해줌. 근데 일부 대부업체가… pic.twitter.com/nfA2rLCtMY

— 펌질하는고닉 (@PJG0012e) November 18, 2026

How Big Is the Gambling Problem in the Army?

The full extent is hard to measure, but Army figures give some indication.

Military police booked 1,721 servicemen on suspicion of online gambling between 2021 and 2025.

That is a small share of an army of more than 320,000 personnel, yet soldiers say betting is far more common among their peers than the official count suggests.

What Do Debt Relief Applications Show?

Requests for help point to growing strain.

The number of active-duty personnel seeking support from the Credit Counseling & Recovery Service stayed in the 400s each year from 2019 to 2021.

It then rose to 753 in 2022 and 1,015 the following year.

A further 322 had applied by April this year, which puts the annual total on course to approach 1,000.

The size of the debts has grown as well.

Average borrowing among servicemen seeking restructuring was 34.01 million won ($24,700) in 2019 and passed 50 million won ($36,300) in 2022.

It reached 58.63 million won ($42,600) as of April this year.

Is This Only a Military Problem?

Experts caution against treating it as one.

Yang Jun-seok, a professor of economics at the Catholic University of Korea, said,

"Debt among servicemen should be understood as part of the broader problem of mounting debt among young people, rather than as an issue unique to the military. Young people are increasingly exposed to financial risks as they take a more active interest in high-risk assets such as cryptocurrencies."

What Else Is the FSS Planning?

Alongside the lending limits, the FSS plans to widen financial education across the armed forces.

That includes more one-on-one counselling and programmes that warn of the dangers of online gambling and leveraged investing.

Starting today, victims of illegal lending in Korea can apply for help online instead of going to a center in person.

Applications are open 24/7 on the Credit Counseling & Recovery Service website or app. Until now, you had to visit one of 22 offices nationwide.

Once you apply,…

— James Kim (@King_James_Kim) November 15, 2026

The regulator also announced wider flexible operations for bank branches and a shorter notification cycle for long-unused prepaid electronic payment accounts, cut from one year to three months.

The token has fallen nearly 40% since election day, briefly touching $0.896 over the weekend. TRUMP Meme Coin Plunges as Political Pressure Mounts

TRUMP touched $0.896 over the weekend, marking its lowest price since launching in January 2025. The token subsequently rebounded approximately 8% to $0.965, but remained nearly 40% below its election-day price and 98.7% below its all-time high of $73.43, reached the day after its launch.

Luke Nolan, senior researcher at CoinShares revealed that the midterm elections had added pressure to an already struggling token. Trading volume increased around the vote, suggesting that some investors had positioned themselves for a potential Republican victory.

However, the election results triggered what Nolan described as a “visible unwind,” contributing to a sharp sell-off as those positions were reversed.

The political fallout could create further challenges for Trump's cryptocurrency ventures. Max Shannon, senior associate at Bitwise Europe, claimed that Democrats taking control of both chambers of Congress in January and potentially using their subpoena powers to investigate Trump's crypto businesses, which could ultimately negatively affect Trump-affiliated assets.

“Democrats take both chambers in January and plan to use their subpoena power on his crypto ventures. His net approval rating has almost never been lower."

President Donald Trump told "60 Minutes" this week he knew “nothing” about the World Liberty Financial crypto company that helped him take in more than $2 billion last year alone. Democrats who’ll take control of Congress in January have big plans to find out more. The incoming heads of various oversight committees are already naming a broad array of investigative targets regarding Trump’s personal and administrative actions. They’re demanding records, promising subpoenas – and warning people and companies not to destroy any documents. 📸: SAUL LOEB/Pool via REUTERS Read more: https://t.co/zIAugNuRm3

— USA TODAY (@USATODAY) November 15, 2026

Other Trump-linked investments have also struggled since the election. World Liberty Financial's WLFI token has declined 7.5%, while shares of Trump Media & Technology Group have fallen 32%, according to Decrypt data.

Trump's cryptocurrency ventures have also attracted political scrutiny surrounding the Clarity Act, legislation intended to establish a formal regulatory framework for much of the cryptocurrency industry. Democrats raised concerns about the Trump family's involvement in crypto businesses, which reportedly generated more than $1 billion in a year.

Fading Demand and Token Unlocks Raise Further Concerns

Beyond political uncertainty, analysts argue that TRUMP faces a more fundamental problem: its limited ability to generate lasting demand.

Shannon described the token as having “no value accrual,” arguing that it has increasingly lost momentum as public interest in the project fades. Google Trends data also shows searches for $TRUMP have remained largely flat since June 2025.

“Right now, if you Google the word ‘idiot’… a picture of Donald Trump comes up. How would that happen?” Google CEO Sundar Pichai faces questions from Congress over Google Search. https://t.co/YeuRL6jUBf

Nolan similarly characterized the token's appeal as “largely speculative,” noting that holding TRUMP does not provide investors with a clear connection to the success of an underlying business.

One of the token's most prominent incentives, exclusive dinners for major holders, has also struggled to maintain interest.
